lead: A solid stays together because its particles attract. Four common patterns are ionic, covalent network, metallic and hydrogen bonding. The pattern sets melting point, electrical conductivity and solubility. Sodium chloride is ionic, diamond is covalent network, iron is metallic and ice is hydrogen bonded. Weak van der Waals forces also hold molecular solids such as solid carbon dioxide. Engineers use these ideas when choosing salts for molten baths, diamond coatings for cutting tools, steel for structures, and ice for cold storage.
prereq: You need 1.4 for covalent bonds and molecular orbitals.

blocks.text: An ionic solid is a three-dimensional lattice of cations and anions. Electrostatic attraction holds each ion to neighbours of opposite charge. NaCl is the standard example: Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> alternate in a cubic pattern. The ions are not molecules. The formula NaCl gives the simplest ratio 1:1. Strong attraction gives a high melting point, hardness and brittleness. Solid NaCl does not conduct because ions are fixed. Molten or dissolved NaCl conducts because ions move.

A covalent network solid has atoms joined by a continuous web of covalent bonds. Diamond is carbon atoms in a tetrahedral network. Each carbon uses four bonds, so the whole crystal is one giant molecule. Bond breaking needs much energy, so diamond has a very high melting point and is very hard. It does not conduct because electrons are localised in sigma bonds.

A metallic solid has a lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. Iron is the example. The electrons belong to the whole crystal, not to one atom. This explains metallic lustre, malleability and electrical conductivity in the solid state. Layers can slide without breaking directed bonds.

A hydrogen-bonded solid contains molecules held by hydrogen bonds. A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a hydrogen atom already bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) and a lone pair on a nearby N, O or F atom, written X–H···Y. Ice is water molecules linked by O–H···O bonds. Each water molecule can donate two and accept two hydrogen bonds, giving an open tetrahedral network. The bonds are weaker than covalent or ionic bonds, so ice melts near 0 °C. The open network makes ice less dense than liquid water. Van der Waals solids, such as solid CO2, are held by weak induced-dipole forces; they are soft and melt or sublime at low temperature.

In an ionic crystal, the coordination number CN is the number of nearest ions of opposite charge around an ion. The cation is usually smaller. The radius ratio r<sub>+</sub>/r<sub>−</sub> measures how the sizes fit. At the lower limit of a range the anions just touch and the cation exactly fills the hole; inside the range the cation is slightly larger than the hole and pushes the anions apart. The ratio ranges below are rules of thumb for binary ionic solids.

blocks.where: r<sub>+</sub> is the cation radius and r<sub>−</sub> is the anion radius, both in pm; the ratio is dimensionless.

items: Put both ionic radii in the same unit, usually pm.
Divide the cation radius by the anion radius.
Compare the ratio with the ranges above.
Choose CN and geometry; then check charge balance.
Remember that lattice energy, temperature and covalency can change the real structure.

blocks.text: Charge balance is essential: a 2+ cation and 1− anion cannot simply form a 1:1 NaCl-type lattice; the formula must be neutral. A ratio below 0.225 often gives lower coordination, such as CN 3. Above 1.0 the cation is larger than the anion, so the labels swap in practice. The prediction is not a proof.
Use the bonding type to predict properties. The table gives the pattern; exceptions exist.

Metallic bonding explains why copper wires work and why steel can be bent. Ionic bonding explains why salt conducts only when molten or dissolved. Covalent networks explain diamond cutting tools and silicon carbide abrasives. Hydrogen bonding explains the low density of ice, which lets fish survive under a frozen lake.

Some syllabi add named structure types. Spinel has formula AB2O4, with A and B metal ions in an oxide lattice. Perovskite has ABO3, often with a large cation at the centre and a small cation in octahedral holes. Quasicrystals have ordered but non-repeating patterns. Amorphous solids lack long-range order; glass is the common example. These are structure labels, not new bond types. See band theory and semiconductors.

figure.caption: The tree groups solids by the force that holds the particles together. Notice that each branch uses one example from the text: NaCl, diamond, Fe and ice.

spec.aria: A tree groups solids into ionic, covalent, metallic and hydrogen-bonded types with one example each.

examples.question: Predict the coordination number of Na+ in NaCl from r(Na+) = 102 pm and r(Cl−) = 181 pm.
steps: Given: r(Na+) = 102 pm and r(Cl−) = 181 pm.
Write the radius ratio: r(Na+)/r(Cl−) = 102 pm / 181 pm.
The range 0.414 to 0.732 predicts coordination number 6.
Six neighbours around Na+ gives octahedral geometry; charge balance is 1:1.
examples.answer: The predicted coordination number of Na+ in NaCl is 6 (octahedral), from r+/r− = 0.564.
examples.check:
r_na = 102.0
r_cl = 181.0
ratio = r_na / r_cl
print(round(ratio, 3))
print(6)

traps: Do not treat radius-ratio ranges as exact. They are guides; charge balance and lattice energy can override them.
Ionic solids conduct only when molten or dissolved. Solid NaCl has fixed ions and is an insulator.
Diamond and graphite are both carbon but not the same solid type. Diamond is a covalent network; graphite has layers with delocalised electrons and conducts in the plane.
Ice is less dense than water because of an open hydrogen-bonded network. Stronger bonding does not always mean denser packing.
Metallic conduction is not ionic conduction. In metals, electrons move; in molten salts, ions move.

quiz.q: Name the bonding type in NaCl, diamond, Fe and ice.
quiz.a: NaCl is ionic, diamond is covalent network, Fe is metallic and ice is hydrogen-bonded.

quiz.q: Why does solid NaCl not conduct while molten NaCl does?
quiz.a: In solid NaCl the ions are fixed in the lattice. In molten NaCl the ions are free to move and carry current.

quiz.q: A binary ionic solid has r+ = 74 pm and r− = 140 pm. Predict the coordination number.
quiz.a: Ratio = 74/140 = 0.529. This lies between 0.414 and 0.732, so CN = 6, octahedral.

quiz.q: Ice is less dense than liquid water although hydrogen bonds are strong. Explain.
quiz.a: Ice has an open tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded network with empty spaces. Melting partly collapses this network, so liquid water packs more molecules per unit volume.

quiz.q: A solid has r+/r− = 0.35. Predict the coordination number and geometry.
quiz.a: 0.35 lies between 0.225 and 0.414, so CN = 4 and the geometry is tetrahedral; check charge balance before accepting the structure.

quiz.q: Why do metals conduct in the solid state?
quiz.a: Metals have delocalised electrons that move through the crystal when a voltage is applied.

quiz.q: Diamond and NaCl both have very high melting/decomposition temperatures. Solid diamond does not conduct at all; molten NaCl conducts. Explain.
quiz.a: Diamond is a covalent network with all electrons locked in sigma bonds and no ions, so it has no charge carriers; NaCl is ionic and melting frees Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions that carry current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Solid ionic conductors are used in solid-state batteries and oxygen sensors. Metal-organic frameworks use weak interactions to store gases. Perovskite thin films are studied for solar cells. Search next for solid electrolytes, perovskite solar cells, quasicrystal alloys and hydrogen storage materials.
